'''Papeda''', or '''''bubur sagu''''', is a type of [[congee]] made from [[sago]] starch. It is a staple food of the people indigenous to [[Eastern Indonesia]], namely parts of [[Sulawesi]],<ref name="Kirana 2020" /> the [[Maluku Islands]] and  coastal [[Western New Guinea|Papua]].<ref name="Femina">{{cite news|title=Papeda, Maluku: Bubur 'Lem' Segar Bergizi |magazine=Femina |language=id |url=http://www.femina.co.id/kuliner/info.kuliner/papeda.maluku.bubur.lem.segar.bergizi/004/002/234 |access-date=9 March 2015}}</ref> It is also widespread in [[Papua New Guinea]] and serves as the counterpart to central and western [[Indonesian cuisine]]s that favour [[rice]] as their staple food.<ref name="Tribun">{{cite news|title=Papeda, Makanan Sehat Khas Papua |date=10 December 2013 |author=Agung BS |magazine=Tribun News |language=id |url=http://www.tribunnews.com/lifestyle/2013/12/10/papeda-makanan-sehat-khas-papua |access-date=9 March 2015}}</ref> Papeda is of [[Ambon Malay]] origin and attested in ''Vocabularium ofte Woort-boeck'' (1623) by Dutch clergymen Caspar Wiltens and Sebastiaan Danckaerts.<ref>{{cite journal |pages=538-9|title=Seventeenth-century Malay wordlists and their potential for etymological scholarship |journal=Wacana, Journal of the Humanities of Indonesia |date=October 2024|first=Tom G. |last=Hoogervorst |url=https://scholarhub.ui.ac.id/wacana/vol25/iss3/7/  |volume=25 |issue=3 |doi=10.17510/wacana.v25i3.1782}}</ref>

The starch is acquired by felling the trunk of a [[Metroxylon sagu|sago palm tree]], cutting it in half, and scraping the soft inner parts of the trunk, the pith, producing a crude sago pith flour. This flour is then mixed with water and squeezed to leach the [[starch]] from the flour. The still-moist sago starch is usually stored in a container made of sago palm leaflets, called ''tumang'', in which it will keep for several months before spontaneous fermentation will turn it too acidic and unsuitable for making papeda. Depending on the variety and the growing conditions, it may take a sago tree five to over ten years to accumulate enough starch in its trunk to make the effort of extracting it worthwhile.<ref>Schuiling, D.L. (2009) ''Growth and development of true sago palm (''Metroxylon sagu ''Rottbøll) with special reference to accumulation of starch in the trunk: a study on morphology, genetic variation and ecophysiology, and their implications for cultivation''. (PhD thesis Wageningen University).</ref>

Papeda is made by cooking sago starch with water and stirring until it coagulates and becomes more translucent. It has a [[glue]]-like consistency and texture.<ref name="Femina"/> ''Sayur bunga pepaya'' (papaya flower bud vegetables) and ''tumis kangkung'' (stir-fried [[water spinach]]) are often served as side-dish vegetables to accompany papeda.<ref name="Tribun"/>
